title: Taylor Townsend, Katerina Siniakova win US Open women's doubles - espn.com
content: NEW YORK -- Taylor Townsend was tight, wasn't moving well and could sense she was swinging her racket early in the US Open women's doubles final. "I wanted this really badly, and I knew that I wanted it," she said. "I felt it in my body and my spirit because I was so nervous." Playing partner Katerina Siniakova talked her through the rough start Friday, and then they found their groove and rolled. Townsend and Siniakova completed their career Grand Slam as a team by defeating the wild-card pair of Ashlyn Krueger and Robin Montgomery for their first US Open doubles title together. "It just means the world to me," Townsend said. "This really means everything to me, not only just to be able to win the US Open but to be able to complete a career Slam." It looked dicey early, when Townsend and Siniakova lost the first three games and dropped the first set. At one point, the ball dropped between them, an uncharacteristic mistake for the top two women's doubles players on the planet. Then the top seeds started looking like it with aggressive shots at the net, and they took control of the match on the way to a 5-7, 6-0, 6-2 victory at Arthur Ashe Stadium. "The match was very tight, very tough for us, but we found a way to win it," Siniakova said. "We found a solution. I'm just really happy that we have this one and we can celebrate it together." The result validated Townsend's confidence in her play after getting knocked out in singles by No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka. The 30-year-old American expressed confidence in her tennis at the time, knowing she still had another opportunity in doubles. That turned into her fourth major championship after she and Siniakova won Wimbledon in 2024, the Australian Open in 2025 and the French Open earlier this year. It was Siniakova's 12th Grand Slam title after winning seven with fellow Czech player Barbora Krejcikova and one with Coco Gauff. "It helps to have someone that's been here so many times and who has been able to get over the hump -- what is it, 12? Twelve times," Townsend said. It was an impressive run for Krueger and Montgomery, who respectively rank 570th and 610th in doubles and went through each half of defending champions Erin Routliffe and Gabriela Dabrowski separately in the quarterfinals and semifinals. Krueger and Montgomery reunited five years after winning the US Open girls' doubles title and advancing a round at the women's level in 2021. "We're both just trying to take it all in," Montgomery said. "What we've just done has been amazing. I think we did forget that we were offered a wild card, so I'm just glad we made good use of it." Townsend and Siniakova, who fell short against Routliffe and Dabrowski in the final a year ago, got a happier result this time. Townsend dropped to her knees after the final point and was all smiles as she said to Siniakova that they finally did it. "If flipping the script had a face," Townsend said, "you'd see my face." A year after famously sipping the tournament's signature cocktail, the Honey Deuce, at the news conference after losing in the women's doubles final, Townsend had one in each hand this time. Carrying just one, Siniakova asked Townsend, "Next year, you have three and I have two?" -- setting the table for the duo to already start thinking about a repeat.

title: “One of the Biggest Statements So Far”: Skatta on Karol G’s “BbY WOW” Global Success - Kaboom Magazine
content: Our latest digital magazine is available for download - CLICK HERE >> “BbY WOW,” which samples the iconic “Coolie Dance Riddim,” gives the classic beat another major global moment. “This beat was different,” Burrell reflects on its enduring impact For years, music producer and industry figure Skatta Burrell has continued to reap the success of his iconic juggling, the Coolie Dance Riddim, as the 2003 production continues to find new life across international music. The compilation, listed by Rolling Stone among the 25 Riddims That Shaped Jamaican Music, became one of dancehall’s biggest international crossovers, powering hits including Elephant Man’s “Jook Gal,” Mr. Vegas’ “Pull Up,” Bounty Killer’s “Yuh Gwan” and more. Its reach stretched even further through Pitbull’s Latin smash “Culo” and Nina Sky’s Billboard Hot 100 Top 10 hit “Move Ya Body,” which was later remixed featuring Vybz Kartel. “The experience of witnessing multiple samples and remixes of the Coolie Dance Riddim is something I’ve been witnessing almost yearly since its release in 2003,” Burrell said, reflecting on the riddim’s longevity. More than two decades later, Coolie Dance continues to move beyond dancehall floors and into the global mainstream. Beyoncé moved to its pulse during her 2023 Renaissance World Tour, while Kehlani sampled the riddim on her 2024 viral hit “After Hours.” Its latest major moment comes through Colombian superstar Karol G, alongside Spanish artistes Judeline and rusowsky, whose “BbY WOW” samples the riddim and climbed to No. 1 on both the Billboard Global 200 and Billboard Global Excl. U.S. charts. The song generated 42.3 million global streams from August 28 to September 3 and has surpassed 116 million streams on Spotify. “This ‘BbY WOW’ hit is by far one of the biggest statements so far, and especially being a Spanish-language song, it seems to be captivating the world due to its infectious melodies and the dynamics and groove from the Coolie Dance beat,” Burrell shared. “No words can explain the gratitude and reassurance I get just knowing I created music that is definitely timeless.” Latin superstar Karol G gives the classic beat another major global moment. For Burrell, the riddim’s continued global success also validates the creative instincts behind a beat that sounded different from much of what surrounded it at the time. “I’ve always known this beat was different and out of the norm, and it reminds me that trying to fit in is never the way to achieving greatness,” he said. “What matters most is the way music makes you feel, and its main purpose is to evoke emotions and movement.” While Burrell admits he never predicted just how far Coolie Dance would travel, he always believed there was more to come from the production. “This global impact was never forecasted. However, I’ve always had that confident assurance inside that there’s always more to come from this Coolie Dance Riddim,” he added. title: How Automation Impacts the Lives and Careers of Displaced Workers - Goldman Sachs

The rapid advance of artificial intelligence (AI) may have significant repercussions for whole occupations. Goldman Sachs Research estimates that 6%-7% of US workers could be “displaced,” meaning they have to find new employment because their roles have been automated, over the next decade. A look at previous waves of technological automation shows that displacement can have lasting effects on workers, hurting their job prospects and even their chances of starting a family. But past examples of technology-driven unemployment also offer some encouragement: Younger workers tend to find it easier to adjust to replacement, and some are able to cushion the impact on their careers by moving into new fields and retraining, Goldman Sachs Research economists Pierfrancesco Mei, Jessica Rindels, and David Mericle write in a report. How does technological displacement impact a worker’s job prospects? Historically, workers who have been displaced by technology have harder job transitions than those in stable or growing occupations. How does technological displacement affect people’s lives outside of work? The scarring effects of technological displacement extend beyond the job market. Workers displaced early in their careers—between the ages of 25-35—accumulate wealth significantly more slowly than other workers. Even the probability of getting married is lower for workers who were displaced by technology. “A key mechanism driving these worse outcomes is occupational downgrading,” Mei, Rindels, and Mericle write. Technology-displaced workers are more likely to move into occupations with more repetitive, rule-based tasks and lower complexity. That’s likely because the same technological changes that eliminated their positions also eroded the value of their existing skills. How can technology-displaced workers improve their job prospects? The impact of technological displacement varies by worker. In short, generative AI is expected to automate a significant share of work tasks across a range of industries. Many workers will benefit from this change, which will boost their productivity and real income; others will lose their jobs as AI takes over a larger share of their work. “Our analysis suggests that, similarly to previous waves of technological change, AI-driven displacement could impose lasting costs on affected workers, worsening labor market outcomes for several years,” write Mei, Rindels, and Mericle. They add that the effects can be “substantially larger” if workers are displaced during a recession. The research shows that retraining programs could help workers cope with these changes, depending on how AI ripples through the job market. These programs may ultimately enable displaced workers to earn modestly higher wages and achieve more stable employment. Yes—historically, technology-displaced workers take roughly one month longer to find a new job than people in stable or expanding occupations, and they suffer three percentage points higher real earnings losses upon reemployment when moving between full-time positions. A decade after they were first made redundant, technology-displaced workers have lower real earnings compared to comparable workers who lost their jobs in non-disrupted occupations. The likelihood of going through a subsequent spell of unemployment is also higher for technology-displaced workers, particularly in the first five years after they are made redundant. Retraining can make it easier to adjust if your role is automated, according to Goldman Sachs Research. Technology-displaced workers who spent at least four weeks in retraining within three years of their job loss achieve roughly two percentage points more cumulative real wage growth in the next decade compared with their peers who did not retrain. They are also less likely to return to unemployment in that period. Yes—recessions tend to intensify technological displacement, as firms shed more routine jobs during a downturn. (NYSE:GS) has opened a new engineering office in Bellevue, Washington, which will house more than 125 employees working on AI and cloud technology. The move gives Goldman a bigger presence in the Pacific Northwest and puts the firm closer to a large pool of technology talent. Goldman already employs more than 12,000 engineers around the world, making up about a quarter of its workforce. The Bellevue office is a good indication that The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. (NYSE:GS) sees AI as something that will play a major role in its business for years, rather than just being another technology trend. Having a dedicated engineering team in a major tech hub should make it easier for Goldman to attract people with experience in AI, cloud computing, and other areas where talent competition is already intense. More engineers focused on AI could also help Goldman automate more of the routine work that takes up employees' time. That could include everything from research and coding to risk management and other internal processes. If Goldman can use AI to help its bankers, traders, and other employees work more efficiently, the firm could potentially get more done without having to increase headcount at the same rate. Over time, that could help keep costs under control and improve margins. Another reason to be positive is that Goldman does not have to figure out how to make money from AI as a standalone business. It can simply use the technology to make the businesses it already has better. AI could help employees analyze information faster, improve client service, automate repetitive tasks, and speed up decision-making. The fact that Goldman is investing in a permanent engineering presence also shows that management appears to be thinking beyond the current AI hype. If the firm can attract good talent and actually put these technologies to work across the business, it could become more efficient and gain an advantage over competitors that are slower to adopt AI. The problem is that all of this will cost money before it starts making money. Hiring highly skilled engineers in the Seattle-area technology market is expensive, and The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. (NYSE:GS) is competing with some of the biggest technology companies for the same people. Salaries and retention costs could therefore add up quickly, while the financial benefits from AI may take several years to become noticeable. There is also no guarantee that Goldman will get a strong return on all of its AI spending. AI technology is changing incredibly quickly, and something the firm invests heavily in today could become outdated sooner than expected. There is also a chance that cheaper third-party AI models could eventually do much of the same work, making some of Goldman's in-house investments less valuable. The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. (NYSE:GS) also has to be more careful with AI than a typical technology company. The firm deals with sensitive financial information and operates under strict regulatory requirements. Cybersecurity, privacy, and the risk of AI making incorrect decisions all have to be taken seriously. That means Goldman cannot simply introduce AI tools as quickly as a tech company might. More testing and oversight could slow down adoption and reduce some of the productivity gains the firm is hoping to achieve. Overall, the Bellevue expansion is a positive step for The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. (NYSE:GS), but the payoff will take time. The new office gives Goldman access to valuable engineering talent and could help the firm make greater use of AI across its existing businesses. If those investments lead to meaningful automation and productivity improvements, they could eventually help Goldman reduce costs and improve profitability. At the same time, investors should not assume that simply spending more on AI will automatically lead to better financial results. Goldman still has to deal with high hiring costs, rapidly changing technology, and strict regulatory requirements. The real test will be whether Goldman can turn its growing AI investment into something investors can actually see in the numbers- higher productivity, lower costs, and stronger profits. title: Andreas Sdrolias’s 1975 Ford XB Falcon GS coupe - Street Machine
content: While there are many events and people that shape our life’s journey, it’s the influences of our teen years that define our tastes for the rest of our lives. For a young Andreas Sdrolias, it was watching the same Falcon hardtop cruise past his bus stop each day on the way to school. First published in the August 2026 issue of Street Machine “Every morning, a steel-blue XC GS coupe rumbled down Anzac Parade,” Andreas recalls. “I was mesmerised by the low roofline and burbling Clevo. I always watched Bathurst and loved the Group C Falcons, especially the coupes. I’d sit at the bus stop waiting for it; I’d let buses go by until I saw that coupe every morning.” With core memories like that seared into his cerebrum, there was never any doubt that Andreas was going to be a Ford guy. After working his way through a few XA sedans and some XE ESP Ghias – including an AIT turbo car that he still owns – Andreas got a line on an XA Superbird for sale, but as luck would have it, he just missed out. Fortunately, luck can be a fickle thing, as the guy selling the Superbird contacted him a few days later about another car near Bundaberg in Queensland. “He rang me back, saying, ‘Would you be interested in an XB coupe?’” Andreas says with a laugh, as if anyone would say no to that question. “He said, ‘My son works for Toyota. He’s a service manager, and this old bloke has just driven in to trade a coupe.’ So, I literally bought it sight-unseen.” Now, Andreas isn’t a crazy person; he asked all the right questions about condition and all that, but when he heard it was a rust-free, Yellow Blaze XB Falcon GS coupe with white trim, he couldn’t transfer the money fast enough. With a 302 Cleveland and an auto transmission, the big Falc wasn’t exactly scorching the roads in terms of performance, but just about everywhere else, it was a perfect cruiser. For the next year or so, Andreas kept the coupe stock. But as we know, the thirst for horsepower is strong, so when he met Bill Kaglatzis from BK Race Engines through a mutual friend, Andreas formulated a plan to quench that thirst via a new powerplant. Initially, the new engine build was a 3V-headed, 383ci Clevo that started off with a hydraulic-roller camshaft, but that was quickly upgraded to a solid-roller after some valve spring issues. That change also saw the horsepower shoot up from 550 to around 640hp, and when combined with a Top Loader four-speed and a nine-inch, the bright yellow XB scooted down the quarter-mile to the tune of 10.88@126mph – stout numbers for a full-weight Falcon back in 2005. Unfortunately, the clutch cried ‘enough’, and as the car had no rollcage, Andreas decided to stick with other high-speed activities like the Snowy Mountains 1000, and Cooma 400 and 500 events. As the years took its toll on the XB’s body and paint, Andreas decided it was time to give ‘Big Bird’ – as the family affectionately call the car – a birthday. So, the 383 engine was sold to a mate, and the shell was sent down to S&K Auto Restorations in Gundagai, where Shane Feltham and his crew could work their magic. The body was straight and almost entirely rust-free, but that didn’t stop Shane from stripping it entirely to bare metal to bring it back to better-than-new condition. After all, 70s Ford Falcons were never file-finished with all the gaps perfectly aligned from the factory, were they? Once the shell was up to scratch, the whole lot was coated in PPG Yellow Blaze and baked until ready. Glowing bright and smooth, the coupe looks like it’s been dipped in sunlight – this is not a vehicle you’ll lose in a carpark. With the plan to add a whole bunch more power, Andreas had a new rear end built using a Strange heavy-duty housing with a bolt-through alloy carrier, which was decked out with a Wavetrac centre, some 4.33:1 gears and a pair of chunky 35-spline axles. If that sounds like overkill, we’ll follow the alloy driveshaft forward to the Tremec T56 Magnum six-speed, with its cryogenically treated gearset and custom twin-plate clutch. But the real meat in this fully loaded souvlaki is the 443ci Clevor between the shock towers. Once again, Andreas had Bill at BK Race Engines crank out a powerhouse, and this time they weren’t mucking about. Using a 9.5in-deck Windsor block, Bill added all the good gear like a Callies crank, Oliver rods, Diamond high-comp pistons and a custom cam with 0.800in lift and all the duration, plus a set of BAM bushed lifters with DLC (diamond-like carbon) coating. This is nothing like your granddad’s 351. Locking in the 13.5:1 comp are a pair of Higgins 2.8 Clevo heads, matched with a Higgins intake and a 1250cfm APD twin-blade carby. Amazingly, it all runs on Premium 98 pump fuel and cranks out 830hp at 8000rpm with 630lb-ft at 5300rpm. This thing has a torque spread like a mountain range, and Andreas has no problem with spinning it all the way out to 8600rpm, which must sound like a heavenly choir with all the angels in attendance. It even featured as Mill Of The Month back in September 2024. “The idea was, let’s build a big V8 Supercar engine,” Andreas reckons. “Something that’s going to be able to pull – you know, dig down and be able to pull a gear, because you haven’t got a converter to make up for it. So, it holds its power, but it’s a baby. It idles at 1000rpm, and I can purr along in traffic in fourth gear.” We spotted the Falcon at this year’s Meguiar’s MotorEx, and Andreas was proud as punch to have the coupe in the big hall wearing its new custom billet rims. But as good as this car looks, it’s no show pony, and Andreas is dead-set on making that stroker small-block sing. “With MotorEx under my belt, it’s time to put some street miles on it, followed by some motorsport,” he says. “I want to do the Flying Fifth at Bathurst, plus the Coota 400 and Muscle Car Challenge, and then finally chase that nine-second timeslip.” THANKSManuel Kapitanos for assembly; Bill at BK Race Engines; Steve for the trim; Pylec; Ignite Auto Electrical; Bill at European Autosports; Yann at JZ Custom Alloy; RaceMax; Deni at Para’s Prestige Detailing; my beautiful wife Afroditi and my family for always supporting me in my car adventures Raised in a house without 240V electricity, at age 16 Scotty was inspired by early issues of Street Machine to build an HQ ute from the chassis up. title: The ADV Bike With BMW GS Comfort And Italian Character - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update Ever since its inception, the boxer GS lineup has attracted thousands of buyers all over the world. The oil-head and hex-head models were quite popular, and the updated wet-head R 1250 GS truly cemented its dominance. The current R 1300 GS and GS Adventure build on that idea, introducing some comprehensive updates in the lineup. These were BMW’s highest-selling bikes last year. However, the base price has risen beyond $20,000, and it breaches $30,000 if you want the full premium bits. That has inevitably opened up the market to rivals, some of which offer a better base package than the GS at a lower starting price. We’re talking about one such bike here, which not only has more oomph than the GS, but it even gets you exotic Italian character. There are a few reasons why the GS lineup has dominated for so long. First and foremost is the reliability. Modern-era boxer-powered GS bikes have always been highly dependable regardless of your use case. Six-digit odometers are common, with very rare major issues. Then, there’s the dollops of performance. Sure, the output isn’t class-leading, but the spread of power is immense, which aids in tractability across terrains. Last but not least is the comfort on offer. BMW’s top-drawer Telelever and Paralever suspension serve as the crown jewels, minimizing dive and unsettling characteristics. That, along with a carefully crafted ergonomic triangle, ensures fatigue is minimal on your tours. A recent addition is the optional Automated Shift Assistant, which means no stress of gear shifts or clutch actuation. As good as all that is, the rivals have truly caught up in recent years. There are worthy alternatives to the GS from all over the world, and even Harley-Davidson whipped up an ADV to rob away sales from the Bavarian company. However, BMW’s biggest headache is from Bologna, offering similar comfort, more power, better technology, and surprisingly, a considerably lower base MSRP. We’re talking about the Ducati Multistrada V4. In base trims, the Multistrada actually offers you more for the money, and this includes comfort. For reference, the base GS has a slim two-up saddle and a puny windscreen, compared to the Multi V4’s visibly larger perch and adjustable windscreen that’s shared with the higher-end variants. In contrast, you need to spend at least $5,000 more if you want the comfier perch on the BMW. Speaking of which, the Multistrada V4 starts at $19,995–an MSRP it has held for a few years, despite a couple of updates in recent times. That makes the Italian ADV $400 cheaper than the base R 1300 GS. That seems like a small difference, but there are some caveats. Firstly, BMW’s official configurator lists the GS’ new base price as $23,795, hinting a large hike for the bike. Secondly, finding a base BMW is like finding a needle in the haystack. We checked several dealers, and the cheapest new R 1300 GS examples we see are equipped with some or the other optional package, taking the total price beyond $24,000. Let’s not forget BMW doesn’t let you pick and choose accessories. Either you get the full $5-6,000 pack, or you don’t get anything. Considering these cases, you’re looking at a net price difference of around $5,000 between the Multi V4 and the GS you actually take home. To make its case stronger, there aren’t any obvious misses for the $19,995 Ducati Multistrada V4. It checks all the boxes you’d expect a premium ADV to, be it in terms of performance, features, or creature comforts. If you feel something is missing, the official accessories take care of that. Let’s dive deeper. If you associate Ducati with Desmo, this is your cue to look away. That’s because the Multistrada V4 boasts a non-Desmo Granturismo engine. This has four cylinders, laid out in a 90-degree V-angle to displace a total of 1,158cc. That helps produce 170 horsepower and 91 pound-feet, where the former is higher but the latter is lower than the twin-cylinder GS. A six-speed transmission sends power to the wheel via a chain final drive. While the absence of desmo valves might feel like a bummer, there are obvious benefits. Firstly, this has allowed Ducati to infuse variable valve timing here. This is said to help spread the power throughout the rev range for extra punch. And having ridden the bike, the system works brilliantly. Next and more important is the service schedule. Ducati’s recommended service interval is a sizable 9,000 miles (or once every two years), while the valve clearance check is at a whopping 37,000 miles. With the V4 engine, Ducati also overhauled the chassis on the Multi V4. Unlike its trellis frame-equipped predecessors, this one has an aluminum monocoque chassis. Ducati says the setup uses learnings from the MotoGP world to ensure sharp handling on the road. When things get rough, the suspension comes into play. Beefy Marzocchi 50 mm USD forks up top and a Sachs monoshock at the rear offer around seven inches of travel. Full adjustability is present to improve versatility, topped with an automatic lowering device at the rear (between 6 and 30 mph). As for wheels and brakes, a 19/17-inch alloy wheel combination is present, each wearing 2x 320 mm and a 280 mm disc, respectively. All that use of aluminum helps Ducati cap the Multistrada V4’s weight at 505 pounds (wet without fuel). That is in the ballpark of its rival, but the seat height is 0.3 inches lower on the Multistrada, thanks to the automatic lowering device. You also get a two-inch longer wheelbase than the GS, which should help with off-road and freeway stability. Being a premium Ducati, there are all the necessary rider aids that improve real-world usability. These are derived from the world of racing, so you know they’ll do their job well. Coming to the package, a six-axis IMU and ride-by-wire allow wheelie control, cornering ABS, and cornering traction control. Ride modes, hill hold, cruise control, and power modes are also present, and so is a two-way quickshifter as standard. Rounding things off is a five-inch TFT display–1.5-inch smaller than the GS. title: The BMW Adventure Bike That Quietly Does Everything Well - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update The past few years have brought a proper overhaul to BMW’s bread-and-butter GS lineup. Not only did the flagships get an overhaul (switching from the 1250 to 1300 platform), but we also got a new entry-level F 450 GS, replacing the largely unsuccessful G 310 GS recently. As a result, the Bavarian brand’s ADV lineup is quite vast today. As much as we dig the choice, the inevitable side effect is that some bikes get less attention. BMW’s cheapest middleweight ADV is a prime example of this. It quietly does everything well, but fails to grab headlines or eyeballs due to its simple nature. Not long ago, the GS lineup started with the G 310 GS, flowed into the F 750, F 800, and F 850 GS. Then came the flagships: the R 1250 GS and R 1250 GS Adventure. Today, though, the cubic capacities have risen across the board to meet new emission norms, resulting in a larger overall lineup capacity-wise that now starts from 450 cc rather than 313 cc. The F 450 GS is the new entry into BMW’s ADV world, powered by a new parallel-twin engine. This has made all the right headlines in recent times, and global reviews only back up the impressive package. At the opposite end is the flagship R 1300 GS duo. These have a new 1,300cc boxer powerhouse and remain the most popular ADVs by the brand. That’s backed up by the sales numbers (they sell the most in the entire BMW lineup). Between these two is the middleweight trio, all of which have the 895cc parallel-twin engine. In this space, it’s the F 900 GS and F 900 GS Adventure that make all the headlines. This is down to their increased rugged appeal and near-class-leading performance. That takes the attention away from their do-it-all sibling, however, which is arguably a more logical F GS for most of us. We’re talking about the F 800 GS. It’s arguably the most vanilla GS in the lineup today, serving as the ‘jack of all trades, master of none’. So you don’t get spoke wheels (even as an option), exotic colorways, or serious off-road prowess. This is why most GS fans don’t consider it in the beginning. But look deeper, and you realize that a 19-inch front wheel for occasional off-road stints, a torque-loaded parallel-twin engine, and likable features are all packaged as standard. That means the 800 GS will happily do commuting, touring, hitting the canyons, or exploring mild trails. Its do-it-all tendencies are convincing enough, but the F 800 GS makes its case stronger via a competitive MSRP. It starts at $10,995 for the Light White colorway, with the Triple Black and Style Sport costing $295 more, respectively. That makes the 800 a sizable $3,400 cheaper than the F 900 GS. It also helps this slot well among less powerful and loaded rivals like the Suzuki V-Strom 800 and Yamaha Tenere 700. Speaking of loaded, the F 800 GS has a likable base package for the price. Let’s dive into it. The engine is arguably the highlight here. This is BMW’s popular parallel-twin powerhouse (with the 270-degree crank) we see on multiple bikes like the F 900 XR, F 900 R, and the F 900 GS duo. Here, the mill is in its most usable tune, producing 87 horsepower and 67 pound-feet. Both numbers peak at just 6,750 RPM, meaning you’ll have ample kick at all times. This also helps promise a fuel efficiency of 55 miles per gallon–a couple more than the 105-HP F 900 GS. You also get a larger four-gallon fuel tank than the F 900 GS’ 3.8-gallon unit, meaning more overall riding range. All the power reaches the wheel via a six-speed transmission, driven by a chain. The two F 900 GS models serve as the extreme kids in the lineup, featuring a 21-inch front wheel and long-travel suspension. But the F 800 GS takes a more neutral approach, just like the do-it-all R 1300 GS. So you get a 19/17-inch alloy wheel combination, paired with a bridge-type steel chassis and a simple suspension setup. The latter comprises telescopic forks and a monoshock, both with 6.7 inches of travel. Only rebound and preload are adjustable at the rear, which is a slight bummer. Twin 305 mm front discs with two-piston Brembo calipers and a rear 265 mm disc with a single-piston caliper make up the brakes. The overall neutral approach also makes the F 800 GS friendlier for the masses dimensionally. The saddle height is low at 32.1 inches, while the wheelbase is tight at 61.3 inches—both measuring less than the F 900 GS. However, its curb weight is 500 pounds, probably due to the extra fuel capacity. This is still in the ballpark of its rivals like the V-Strom 800. Although this is the cheapest midweight GS, the feature list is comparable to its F 900 siblings. A 6.5-inch TFT is front and center, armed with BMW Motorrad Connectivity. It also serves as the gateway to the rider aids, comprising cornering ABS (or ABS Pro as BMW calls it), dynamic traction control, and two ride modes. Topping this is a likable set of creature comforts like heated grips, cruise control, USB ports, adjustable levers, and all-LED lights. BMW mentions these as 'standard' inclusions in 2026, although these were previously part of the options list. If you choose the Triple Black and Style Sport colorways, you also get a taller, adjustable windscreen. Lastly, we also want to give a shoutout to the design. Unlike the distinct-looking 900 GS, the 800 GS still has the likable OG GS elements. The geometrical headlight shape is one, while the angular side fairings and front beak are other notable bits. These remind us of the ultra-popular R 1250 GS. As mentioned earlier, there are some things the F 800 GS does better than the F 900 GS, and in some aspects, it’s the other way around. So, which of the middleweight GS models is right for your riding style? If you’re on a budget and want to experience a middleweight GS with an easy-to-ride, underrated parallel-twin engine on the market today, the F 800 GS is for you. At $10,995, it is $3,400 cheaper than the F 900 GS. The next decision is how much dirt you are planning to tackle. If most of your rides are on-road with an occasional dirt road along the way, then the F 800 GS is for you. It is an adventure tourer that will feel more comfortable on the road. Another point is that the F 800 GS is the more approachable of the two motorcycles, given that it produces almost 20 ponies less than the F 900 GS. However, its weight will negate some of that approachability for newer riders to the segment. On the other hand, the F 900 GS absolutely stands out as an enduro adventurer. It’s a high-performance, lightweight ADV that can handle serious off-roading. It’s also equipped with fully adjustable top-shelf suspension, so you can dial it in as per the occasion. While more expensive, the F 900 GS is ideal if you want a middleweight Beemer that can handle everything from on-road duties to serious off-roading. We can’t ignore the F 900 GS Adventure, sitting at the very top. While built on the F 900 GS, the Adventure variant is a heavy-duty mile-muncher. It features the same 105-horsepower power output and is around 60 pounds heavier than the F 900 GS, but it makes up for it with its massive 6-gallon fuel tank, better wind protection, and optional Dynamic ESA electronic suspension. Get this if you plan to ride the breadth of the continent with some off-roading along the way. We want to hear from you. title: Dark Knight Boxer: Kevils Speed Shop’s BMW R nineT Urban G/S - Bike EXIF
content:
Operating out of Paignton, Devon, along the coastal stretch of southwest England affectionately known as the English Riviera, Kevils Speed Shop has been a fixture of the custom scene since founder Kevin Hill opened its doors in 2010. Having cut its teeth on classic BMW airheads with well over 100 builds under its belt, the workshop gained international renown for building bikes for high-profile clients, including preparing Charley Boorman’s BMW R75/5 for an Arctic journey alongside Ewan McGregor. These days, Kevils operates on an unusual dual model known as Kevil's Kitchen & Speedshop: part custom motorcycle workshop, part street-food eatery serving burgers alongside retro biker culture. "It makes for an unusual combination, but motorcycles and burgers seem to work rather well together," jokes owner Kevin Hill. As the custom landscape evolved, Kevin shifted his focus from classic airheads toward modern machinery, particularly BMW’s modular R nineT platform. After BMW Motorrad UK invited Kevils to customize an R nineT for its stand at Birmingham’s NEC Motorcycle Live in 2014, the shop went on to build roughly 20 custom R nineTs. That rich pedigree brought a client from the north of England to Devon with a pristine, low-mileage 2019 BMW R nineT Urban G/S and a simple, evocative brief: build a motorcycle inspired by Batman. Movie and comic book themed custom motorcycles are notoriously difficult to execute. Too often, pop-culture builds devolve into tacky novelty props, heavy on plastic, fragile bodywork, and gimmicks that age poorly and ruin real-world rideability. Rather than relying on cartoonish graphics or bat logos, Kevin interpreted the prompt through stance, texture, and menace. "I wanted to create a motorcycle that was perfectly at home on the streets of Gotham City," Hill explains. The goal was to preserve the Urban G/S’s everyday usability while retaining the grunt of its 1,170 cc air/oil-cooled boxer twin and giving it a brooding, anti-hero aesthetic. Think Christian Bale’s Dark Knight rather than Adam West. For the first step in giving the motorcycle its atheistic , Kev installed a proprietary solo-seat conversion. Stripping away the factory rear bodywork radically shortened the bike’s visual footprint, shedding bulk while exposing the rear frame and the Öhlins rear shock. The handmade solo seat was upholstered in diamond-stitched grey leather, creating a slim, floating line that contrasts with the stock fuel tank. A tiny LED tail light was integrated beneath the seat base to keep the rear end clutter-free. Up front, the factory suspension remains internally stock, but custom fork guards were fitted to give the front end a wider, more muscular silhouette. Clamped between the triple trees sits a compact LED headlight housed within a custom, Bat-inspired nacelle equipped with a protective mesh grille, accompanied by a small auxiliary spot lamp. To back up the aggressive styling, Kevin discarded the stock airbox in favor of a pair of DNA pod filters. To ensure clean power delivery across the rev range, fueling was remapped using a Rapid Bike Evo module. Exhaust gases now exit via a pair of custom, straight-through pipes, one running down each side of the swingarm, allowing the boxer motor to bark freely. Unsurprisingly, almost every surface was refinished in black. By mixing matte, satin, and gloss finishes across the engine, frame, and bodywork, Kevin ensured the monochromatic theme retained depth rather than looking flat or washed out. The build was completed in roughly six weeks, achieved in focused evening stints after Kevin finished long days flipping burgers in the shop’s food truck. The result is a refined, perfectly proportioned daily rider. "It fulfilled the original Batman brief without becoming theatrical, and it retained the reliability and usability expected of a modern BMW," says Hill. Executing a character-inspired build without falling into tacky pop-culture tropes is a challenge, but Kevils Speed Shop nailed the brief with restraint. By prioritizing rideability, clean proportions, and subtle monochromatic textures, Kevin Hill turned a modern boxer twin into a brooding, street-legal weapon. It may be proof that with a steady supply of burgers, an everyday German adventure-tourer can seamlessly step into the shadows of Gotham. Batman?

title: Skatta Burrell Hits #1 on Billboard Global 200 as Karol G's 'BbY WOW' Samples 'Coolie Dance Riddim' - DancehallMag
content: A 23-year-old riddim just topped the Billboard Global 200. That is the story behind Karol G’s “BbY WOW,” which samples Skatta Burrell’s “Coolie Dance Riddim” and has now carried the Jamaican producer to the very top of one of music’s most competitive global charts. Karol G made the track alongside Judeline and rusowski, and the combination landed hard. BbY WOW” has crossed 100 million streams on Spotify and is currently sitting at number 16 on the Billboard Hot 100, meaning this is not just a viral moment but a sustained chart run. For Skatta Burrell, this is a full-circle moment that few producers get to experience. The “Coolie Dance Riddim” originally dropped in the early 2000s, and the fact that it is now fueling a global hit in 2025 says a lot about the staying power of classic dancehall production. There is a broader conversation happening here too. Every time a Latin or pop artist reaches back into the dancehall catalog and scores a massive hit, it reopens the debate about credit, compensation, and how the genre’s originators are recognized when their work travels this far. Skatta Burrell has been vocal in celebrating the achievement, and the dancehall community has largely rallied around the news with genuine pride. Seeing a riddim from Kingston’s golden era land at the top of a chart that spans every genre and every market is not something that happens every cycle. What makes this particularly interesting is the generational bridge it creates. Younger listeners discovering “BbY WOW” through Karol G’s fanbase are now getting pulled toward the original riddim, which is exactly the kind of organic discovery that keeps classic sounds alive rather than just sampled and forgotten. Karol G has built a reputation for pulling from unexpected sonic spaces, and this choice reflects a real ear for what makes a groove feel both fresh and rooted. The “Coolie Dance Riddim” has that low-end bounce that translates across languages and scenes, which is probably why it worked so well underneath a Spanish-language pop record in 2025. The New Taipei City Government on Tuesday unveiled a GS safety certificate system for pet products in collaboration with private enterprises in the industry. Incidents involving animal harm by unsafe pet products prompted the city’s Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office to develop a safety labeling system based on policies that foreign countries successfully implemented, office Deputy Commissioner Liu Hsu-fen (劉淑芬) told a news conference. Pet products using substandard materials or of poor construction pose a danger to pets, Liu said. Establishing safety standards and inspection protocols helps manufacturers to design better products and identify potential flaws to prevent harm, said Huang Hsien-ping (黃獻平), chairman of the Taipei-based China Pet Products Development Association. The GS standard obliges manufacturers to report unsafe products to the association for recall and comply with measures should a major safety incident occur, Huang said. Office Director Yang Shu-fang (楊淑方) said pet owners should think carefully about their pet’s size, physical condition, age and habits before buying products. Protecting the welfare of pets requires a regulatory system that provides comprehensive oversight from design to safety evaluation before products are released to the consumer market, an office spokesperson said. New Taipei City Government officials and association representatives at the news conference demonstrated how to check the suitability of a product for pets. title: Mr. G’s scoops up gold in Gettysburg Connection’s summer ice cream contest - Gettysburg Connection
content:
The votes are in, and the results are as sweet as expected: Mr. G’s has won the gold medal in Gettysburg Connection’s summer ice cream contest, with Half Pint Creamery’s Gettysburg location earning silver and Kilwins in Gettysburg taking bronze. Readers cast hundreds of votes on our local business listing pages to recognize their favorite places to cool off with a frozen treat. Gold medalist Mr. G’s, at 404 Baltimore St., serves homemade ice cream, soft serve, milkshakes and sundaes at the historic Twin Sycamores house. Owners Marc and Megan McLean continue a business tradition that began in 1997. The shop has occupied its current location since 2011, offering customers a place to enjoy their ice cream beneath the branches of a sycamore witness tree. Silver medalist Half Pint Creamery offers homemade, hand-dipped ice cream, with a rotating selection of flavors alongside classic favorites. Its Gettysburg shop has recently moved to 1153 Biglerville Road, where customers will find indoor and outdoor seating and parking. The creamery also offers ice cream cakes, sandwiches and cupcakes. Bronze medalist Kilwins, at 37 Steinwehr Ave., pairs its Original Recipe Ice Cream with an assortment of sweets. Customers can also choose from handmade fudge, chocolates, truffles and chocolate-covered treats, making the shop a stop for both a scoop to enjoy while strolling through Gettysburg and a box of sweets to take home. title: Small-scale fishermen seek clarification of FAO D-G’s remarks - fiskerforum.com
content:
FAO director-general Qu Dongyu is under pressure to clarify comments made at the recent World Summit on Small-Scale Fisheries held in Rome, when he stated that we ‘certainly do not need more wild fish catches,’ and questioned the nutritional quality of wild fish, portraying fishing as an activity that is generally neither sustainable nor environmentally friendly, nor capable of generating sufficient income. A joint statement was prepared in response within the framework of the International Planning Committee for Food Sovereignty (IPC) to express the concerns of fishing communities and Indigenous Peoples over the director-general’s comments, in which he also advocated for a more intensive and technologically advanced form of aquaculture, claiming this could produce more and faster than nature. Delegates see this as a productivist vision that ignores the environmental and social impacts of industrial aquaculture, as well as the essential role of fishermen, their knowledge, and their territories. According to the director-general’s remarks, the idea wild fish is better than farmed fish is, from a scientific point of view, ‘absurd,’ stating that wild fish grow too slowly and feed irregularly, unlike farmed fish the growth of which can be accelerated and controlled using artificial intelligence and digital tools, and which, he stated, could produce much higher incomes on a single hectare of fresh or salt water. ‘Hearing such remarks from the highest-ranking official of the FAO is extremely worrying. Hearing them at a summit specifically dedicated to artisanal fisheries is a real affront to the women and men who have depended on fishing for their livelihoods, feeding communities, and caring for aquatic ecosystems for generations. The fishermen present were not fooled. Many felt directly devalued and offended,’ a small-scale fishing representative commented. ‘Presenting accelerated fish growth and increased production volumes as progress in itself reflects a dangerously simplistic view of aquatic food systems. This approach ignores ecological limits, animal welfare, nutritional quality, the social and environmental consequences of industrial models, and the rights of communities that depend on aquatic environments. Nature is not a competitor that technology should surpass. It is the living foundation of our food systems, our cultures, our territories, and our livelihoods.’ The small-scale organisations point out that beyond the immediate outrage, this raises profound political concerns of how can small-scale fishers can have confidence in the international commitments made on their behalf when the FAO Director-General himself delivers speeches that devalue wild fish, capture fisheries, and community knowledge? ‘The FAO is the custodian of the Voluntary Guidelines for Sustainable Small-Scale Fisheries. It therefore has a particular responsibility: to advocate for their implementation, recognise the rights of fishing communities and Indigenous Peoples, and support food systems based on their knowledge, their territories, and their meaningful participation in decision-making,’ a stakeholder representative said. ‘An institution tasked with fighting hunger and supporting artisanal fishing cannot promote a vision that pits technology against nature, devalues wild fish, and presents industrialisation as the sole path to development. Fishermen’s organisations now expect a clear and public response from the FAO, commensurate with the affront they feel and the profound concern caused by these statements.’ All pictures, texts and data on FiskerForum are protected by Danish copyright law. Audi has long been a formidable presence in the segment, and Mercedes perfected the "German muscle car" with their V8-powered AMGs, but credible non-German challengers have always been rare. What makes the landscape even more challenging is that the market has been shifting decisively away from traditional performance vehicles. Sports cars are few and far between, coupes that are not dedicated sports cars are nearly extinct, and SUVs and crossovers have become the default choice for most buyers. The SUV craze began in the late 1990s and early 2000s, with pioneers like the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V anchoring the economy end of the spectrum, while the Mercedes-Benz ML and the Lexus RX300 effectively invented the modern luxury crossover class. We've added more insights into what makes this sedan's V8 engine special and how to extract more power from it without ruining its character. With crossovers now the industry standard, performance cars have had to evolve in tandem. You can't build a performance variant of a vehicle you no longer sell — and since automakers are moving crossovers the way McDonald's moves burgers and fries, while sedans are quietly fading like Circuit City and RadioShack, it only makes sense that the ranks of performance sedans and coupes have thinned considerably. There is nothing inherently wrong with something like the X5M, but performance sedans have always held a special appeal for enthusiasts that no SUV has quite managed to replicate. Thankfully, there are still some fantastic performance sedans on the market — but there is one in particular that deserved to stick around a little longer. The muscle car is American, the exotic sports car Italian, and the performance saloon German. Obviously, this is a generalization, but such widely held perceptions of certain market segments have a real impact on how consumers shop. A common critique levied at something like the Genesis G90 is that it isn't quite up to the standard of the S-Class. That isn't entirely untrue, but buyers often begin their evaluation of a Genesis, Acura, Cadillac, or Lexus by assuming it could never surpass a “proper” German luxury sedan. While American, Japanese, and Korean automakers have all built exceptional luxury and performance sedans, overcoming those deeply ingrained perceptions remains an uphill battle. Much like General Motors and John DeLorean inventing the muscle car in 1964, BMW ostensibly invented the modern sports sedan in 1984 with the introduction of the E28 M5. The first-ever M5 was powered by a 3.5L I6 that produced 256 horsepower in the North American market. The iconic E30 M3 arrived just two years later, and two years after that the second-generation M5, the E34, upped displacement to 3.6L (3.8L post-facelift in Europe) and pushed output past 300 horsepower. And if the E34 didn't cement the M5 legacy, the legendary 4.9L V8-powered E39 most certainly did. Mercedes followed suit in 1993 with the first production AMG, the C36. In the years that followed, some incredible cars continued the lineage — the C36 gave way to the V8-powered C43, C55, and C63. The E39 was succeeded by the 5.0L V10-powered E60, and Audi was busy fitting V8s and V10s into its S and RS cars throughout the 2000s. Just as the Mustang defined the pony car, these German sports sedans defined their segment, making it that much harder for outside competitors to carve out a lasting place. Find a car enthusiast and ask them which sports sedan on the current market would be their pick. If you ask me? I'll take a Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing, thank you very much. And it's not just because you get a 6.2L supercharged V8 producing 650 horsepower — borrowed from the C7 Z06 — paired with the brilliant MagneRide suspension. No, despite my great appreciation for many automatics, I simply prefer a manual transmission. I'm certainly not in the minority, and aside from the M3, Cadillac is the only other game in town when it comes to rowing your own gears in a four-door sedan. No manual has been offered in the M5 since the F10 generation, and no manual has appeared in an Audi sports sedan since the B8.5 S4 — or the B7 RS4 if you want the full-fat performance model. Cadillac, meanwhile, offers both the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing with 6-speed manuals. The CT5-V Blackwing is the spiritual heir to the original V-car, the CTS-V. When it arrived in 2004 with the 405-horsepower LS6 V8 borrowed from the C5 Corvette Z06, it was the last thing anyone expected from Cadillac. At the time, the brand was riding high on the second-generation Escalade and still selling the DeVille and Seville. There was already plenty of surprise in 2003 when the CTS 3.6L became the first Cadillac offered with a manual transmission since the 1988 Cimarron — nobody was expecting the original CTS-V on top of that, let alone a second generation that paired a manual transmission with 556 supercharged horsepower from the LSA V8. We're quite lucky the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing models have carried that torch, because the Pontiac GXP and Chevy SS came and went faster than the Honda Prologue. The Cadillac offerings have been among the absolute best in this segment for the better part of two decades. The CTS-V and ATS-V — and their successors, the CT4-V and CT5-V Blackwing — are arguably even better than their respective M5 and M3 counterparts, proving that American brands have a legitimate claim in this space. Japanese and Korean brands have made attempts, but have struggled to establish a long-term foothold. Aside from Lexus, Infiniti and Genesis are the only two of the bunch to have offered a V8, but the M56/Q70 5.6L and G80 5.0L fall well short of true sports sedan status. The Kia Stinger GT2, Genesis G70 3.3T, Infiniti Q50 Red Sport, and Acura TLX Type S are all fantastic cars, but they compete more directly with cars like the S4, M340i, C43 AMG, and the CT4-V (non-Blackwing) than with M Division, AMG, or Blackwing at the top. Lexus is really the only one of the bunch to have genuinely gone after BMW — first with the IS-F, and then with one of the all-time great performance sedans. The GS-F was based on the fourth-generation Lexus GS, introduced in 2011. Unlike the previous generation of GS, which offered V8 trims such as the GS 400, 430, and 460, the final iteration of the Lexus GS was V6-only. It was an excellent V6 — the 3.5L 2GR-FE/FKS — but it didn't quite pack the punch of the V8 cars. That's fine, though, because for the final generation Lexus saved the V8 for something more special: the GS-F. While the previous V8 trims were essentially engine upgrades, the GS-F was a proper sports sedan. It was Lexus's second entry into that market, following the 2008–2014 IS-F. It used the same 8-speed automatic and 5.0L V8 as the IS-F, but produced 51 more horsepower than its predecessor. And as noted, the GS-F is far more than just an engine. Starting in 2017, models received adaptive variable suspension (AVS), which allows the car to adjust the dampers independently across 30 different settings based on driver input, selected mode, and real-time sensor data. All GS-F models also received a torque-vectoring differential that can be set to standard, slalom, or track mode. This is not to be confused with brake torque vectoring, as found on a Fiesta ST — this is a proper mechanical trick diff that automotive journalists consistently praised for allowing this large sedan to rotate through corners like a much smaller machine. The GS-F was also fitted with Brembo 6-piston front and 4-piston rear brakes, giving the driver genuine confidence when scrubbing off speed. The GS-F shares the same wonderful powertrain as the IS-F and RC-F, using the same Aisin AA80E 8-speed automatic — though the GS-F has a shorter final drive ratio than the IS-F and RC-F — and the 2UR-GSE 5.0L V8. Which is to say, it works. The AA80E, which debuted in the 2007 LS 460 as the world's first production 8-speed automatic, has earned an excellent long-term reputation. It most recently appeared in the IS 500 F Sport Performance, which shares the same mechanical core as the proper F models. Both the 2UR-GSE and the Aisin 8-speed are genuinely reliable units. In fact, the entire car is, which is why these have held 60%–70% of their value since new. According to classic.com and comparable sales from major auction sites, the GS-F is currently valued at nearly double that of an equivalent M5 from the same era, despite the performance gap. It's true that contemporary rivals — the aforementioned M5, CTS-V, E63, and RS7 — all made more power and could outpace the GS-F's already brisk 4.4-second sprint to 60 mph. That was a legitimate critique when the car was new, but 467 horsepower and 389 lb-ft of torque are not small numbers. We've been desensitized to power figures that include a comma, but a 193-inch, 4,100-pound sedan reaching 60 mph in the same time as a 981 Cayman S is genuinely impressive. And besides — are you really taking this to the track? Are you racing for pinks? The GS-F may not have been the outright performance king of its era, but given its reliability and its glorious engine note, it deserved another chance. It only lasted five model years, after all. Sadly, though it's possible Toyota could one day fit the 4.0L twin-turbo V8 from the GR GT3 into a new Lexus sports sedan, the sedan market may not survive long enough for that to happen. Lexus currently only offers the front-wheel-drive ES in the sedan segment. Thankfully, the GS-F appears reliable enough to last for decades — just don't expect prices to fall; the market has already figured out how special these cars are. It's just a shame there won't be another. Fun Fact: Before the GS F reached showrooms, Lexus engineers subjected it to the Nürburgring Nordschleife, Fuji Speedway, and Autopolis, using some of the world's toughest circuits to sharpen its handling and performance. Part of the reason the GS F feels so special is hiding under its hood:     Toyota's 2UR-GSE, widely regarded as one of the automaker's finest modern naturally aspirated engines. Rather than relying on forced induction like most of its rivals, Lexus built this 5.0-liter V8 around high-rpm breathing, sharp response, and durability. The formula starts with free-breathing cylinder heads developed by Yamaha, while lightweight forged connecting rods and titanium intake and exhaust valves help the V8 spin to a 7,300-rpm redline. The D-4S fuel system combines direct and port injection, allowing the engine to run a high 12.3:1 compression ratio without sacrificing everyday drivability. VVT-iE adds another clever trick. During steady cruising, the engine can run the Atkinson cycle for better efficiency; step on the gas, and it switches to the Otto cycle for stronger performance. The GS F may have looked outgunned by German rivals on paper, but that misses the point. The 2UR-GSE was engineered for immediacy, revs, and character—not a dyno-sheet arms race. It's a big V8, but it was developed with a surprisingly sophisticated purpose. What if you want more than 467 horsepower from your GS F? The car's output was always a sore spot beside 600-horsepower     German sports sedans, and while Lexus made up ground with refinement and character, some owners will still want more. Fortunately, the 2UR-GSE has powered several Lexus performance models since the 2000s, giving it a healthy aftermarket. One upgrade is the RR Racing-tuned PPE header, which RR Racing estimates can add 25–35 whp, or 40–48 whp when paired with its tune. Freer-flowing exhaust components, intake upgrades, and ECU calibration can build on those gains. The catch is that a naturally aspirated V8 doesn't respond like a turbo engine. There is no boost pressure to turn up, so gains come from improving airflow, combustion, and calibration rather than simply increasing boost. That makes the smartest GS F builds less about chasing a giant dyno number and more about making this already special V8 breathe and respond even better. Luxury performance sedans are notorious for shedding value once they leave the showroom. The Lexus GS F hasn't escaped depreciation entirely, but it has aged far more gracefully on the used market than its German rivals. With an original MSRP ranging from about $84,440 for 2016 models to more than $90,000 for a well-optioned 2020 example, the GS F has become more attainable over time, yet it remains remarkably resistant to the steep value drops that typically define this segment. Today, early 2016–2017 cars typically trade anywhere from the high-$30,000s to around $50,000, depending on mileage and condition, while facelifted 2018–2020 examples — which received updated styling and additional standard technology — regularly command well over $50,000. Exceptional low-mileage cars can fetch considerably more, as demonstrated by a 20,000-mile 2020 GS F that sold for $73,500 on Bring a Trailer in early 2025. Meanwhile, buyers can still pick up an F10 BMW M5 for less than $30,000, and even the rare S212 Mercedes-Benz E 63 AMG often changes hands for under $40,000. The contrast highlights just how well the GS F has protected its value. Lexus' hard-earned reputation for reliability is undoubtedly part of the equation, but it's far from the only reason. Lexus' reputation for bulletproof reliability is certainly part of the reason the GS F has depreciated far less than its European rivals, but it's far from the whole story. There are other reasons, starting with sheer rarity. The collector market tends to reward cars that combine genuine performance with genuine scarcity, and the Lexus GS F checks both boxes. While BMW and Mercedes-AMG built their M5 and E63 in far greater numbers, Lexus produced roughly 4,823 GS Fs worldwide during the model's five-year run, with only about 2,347 examples reaching U.S. buyers. Special editions and uncommon specifications only amplify that exclusivity — the 2019 10th Anniversary Edition was capped at 100 U.S. cars, while rare finishes such as Flare Yellow and Molten Pearl have become especially sought-after among enthusiasts. Just as important is what's under the hood. The GS F's 5.0-liter 2UR-GSE V8 belongs to a rapidly shrinking breed of naturally aspirated performance engines, particularly in the sports sedan world. It rewards drivers with immediate throttle response, a broad and predictable power curve, a 7,300-rpm redline, and an exhaust note that no turbocharged engine can quite replicate. Those qualities are even more compelling today, given that there is no naturally aspirated V8 sports sedan currently on sale. After spending so much time praising the GS F, it's fair to ask why Lexus discontinued it after the 2020 model year. The answer has less to do with the GS F itself and more to do with the fate of the GS sedan it was built upon. By the end of its run, the GS had become financially unsustainable. Lexus sold just 3,378 GSs in the U.S. during 2019, accounting for only 4% of the brand's passenger-car sales and less than 1% of the midsize luxury sedan segment. The GS was also squeezed from both sides. Buyers seeking comfort overwhelmingly chose the less expensive ES, while those wanting practicality flocked to the RX, which routinely sold well into six figures annually. With engineering resources increasingly directed toward crossovers, the aging fourth-generation GS received only incremental updates, leaving its interior technology and overall package trailing newer European competitors. As impressive as the GS F was, it couldn't reverse those trends. Against 600-plus-horsepower twin-turbo rivals like the BMW M5 and Mercedes-AMG E 63, its 467-horsepower naturally aspirated V8 appealed to a niche audience. Combined with Lexus' smaller performance-brand footprint, the GS F simply wasn't enough to save the GS nameplate. The GS F belongs to a category that has effectively disappeared. You can no longer walk into a dealership and buy a naturally aspirated V8 sports sedan. Nearly every manufacturer has downsized to turbocharged six-cylinder engines or electrified powertrains in pursuit of stricter emissions targets and improved fuel economy. Even the remaining V8-powered performance sedans rely almost exclusively on forced induction to achieve their staggering power figures. They are undeniably quicker, but they lack the immediate throttle response, progressive power delivery, and intoxicating high-revving character that defined the GS F. To its credit, Lexus kept that philosophy alive a little longer with the IS 500 F SPORT Performance. Sharing the GS F's 5.0-liter 2UR-GSE V8, the smaller sedan produced a slightly improved 472 horsepower and wrapped it in a lighter, more agile package that many enthusiasts considered the spiritual successor to the GS F. The IS 500 F SPORT Performance demonstrated that Lexus still believed there was an audience for a naturally aspirated V8 luxury sports sedan, but it ultimately proved not large enough to overcome market realities.     Production ended after the 2025 model year, bringing Lexus' naturally aspirated V8 sedan lineage to a close. As emission regulations tighten and electrification accelerates, cars like the GS F are becoming relics of a different era. Enthusiasts continue to ask for naturally aspirated V8 sports sedans, but the industry is moving in a different direction. That only makes the GS F more desirable today — not just as a great driver's car, but as a reminder of a performance philosophy that may never return. title: Goldman's IG Deal Expands Canadian Wealth Reach & AWM Scale - tradingview.com
content: In sync with its broader effort to scale Asset & Wealth Management (“AWM”) and increase the contribution of recurring, fee-based revenues, The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. GS entered a strategic collaboration with IG Wealth Management to expand its presence in the Canadian wealth-management market. Under the agreement, Goldman Sachs Asset Management’s multi-asset solutions team will assume portfolio-management responsibilities for five IG Strategic Wealth Portfolios. The portfolios provide Canadian investors exposure to diversified strategies spanning equities, fixed income and alternatives. Over the past several years, Goldman has been focused on building a larger, capital-light AWM franchise and reducing its dependence on more volatile, balance-sheet-intensive revenues. wealth management, alternatives and solutions have been identified as three major growth opportunities within AWM. Management and other fees, together with private banking and lending revenues, saw a compound annual rate of 12% from 2021 through 2025, with the rising trend continuing in the first half of 2026, highlighting the increasing importance of durable revenues to Goldman’s earnings mix. Goldman has supported this strategy through partnerships and targeted acquisitions. In September 2025, it partnered with T. Rowe Price TROW to develop public-private investment solutions for wealth and retirement clients. Goldman also acquired Innovator Capital Management in April 2026, adding about $31 billion in assets under supervision and strengthening its defined-outcome ETF capabilities. In August 2026, it agreed to acquire NEOS Investments, which manages roughly $30 billion. Together, NEOS, Innovator and Goldman’s existing operations are expected to create a $130-billion global ETF platform, expanding its reach among advisors and wealth-management clients. GS entered an agreement in August 2026 to acquire LCN Capital Partners, adding a specialist investment platform focused on sale-leaseback, build-to-suit and triple-net-lease real estate investments. Collectively, these moves demonstrate Goldman’s strategy of adding differentiated investment capabilities that can attract third-party assets and generate recurring management fees. Overall, the IG Wealth Management collaboration underscores Goldman’s continued focus on scaling AWM and building a more durable revenue base. Alongside the T. Rowe Price partnership and the Innovator, NEOS and LCN transactions, the latest collaboration strengthens GS’s third-party distribution capabilities and broadens its addressable wealth-management market. Over time, successful expansion of these relationships should support recurring fee growth, improve the quality of Goldman’s revenue mix and further advance its transition toward a more capital-light business model. Two close peers of GS are JPMorgan JPM and Morgan Stanley MS, which are also making efforts to expand their AWM businesses. JPMorgan’s AWM segment is a steadier, fee-led profit engine inside the bank, spanning asset management and the private bank. For the first half of 2026, the segment’s revenues rose 15% from the year-ago period. As of June 30, 2026, JPMorgan’s assets under management were $5.14 trillion, up 18% year over year, while client assets increased 19% to $7.66 trillion. Morgan Stanley’s AWM push is more than a diversification story. For the first half, Wealth Management revenues and Investment Management revenues were $20.6 billion, nearly half of Morgan Stanley’s $41.9 billion in firmwide net revenues. As of June 30, 2026, total client assets across Wealth Management were $8.08 trillion, while assets under management or supervision reached $2 trillion under the Investment Management division. title: GS Department of World Languages and Cultures professor named executive director of national French honor society, Pi Delta Phi - Grice Connect
content: In early August, French Professor Olga Amarie, Ph.D., in Georgia Southern University’s Department of World Languages and Cultures, was named the newest executive director of the board of Pi Delta Phi, the oldest national academic honor society for a world language within the United States. The organization also provides opportunities for students to connect with leading scholars in French studies and assists students in applying for study abroad scholarships. However, Amarie’s involvement extends beyond her current title. “I joined Pi Delta Phi as a graduate student at the University of Notre Dame, chapter Mu Phi. It is not common for European universities to have honor societies for each specific field. It was completely new and interesting for me as an international student,” she said. In 2012, Amarie took her commitment to the organization and the students it serves a step further. “Dr. David Seaman, emeritus, advised me to visit the Pi Delta Phi board at the Rocky Mountain Modern Language Association Conference because they had an open session, which I did,” Amarie said. “Soon after, I volunteered to serve as vice president for the society and opened nine chapters of Pi Delta Phi,” Amarie said. Although this is her first time with the Executive Director title, this veteran educator has spent more than three decades devoting her career to supporting future generations of French scholars. “The responsibilities are new but something I like to do: maintain all sorts of records for the society; represent the society at the annual meeting of the Association of College Honor Societies; work with chapter moderators on Pi Delta Phi materials; and work with scholarship recipients who will study abroad in Chicoutimi, Canada, and in Paris, Aix-en-Provence, France, etc.,” Amarie said. As technology continues to rapidly evolve, Amarie stresses the importance of world culture and language as an integral part of human connection, scholarship and meaningful advancement. “Many employers value multilingual employees. I personally speak four languages: Romanian, French, English and Russian. Foreign language skills are useful in many fields, including education, business, health care, government, tourism, international relations and technology. Being bilingual or multilingual can make job candidates more competitive,” she said. Looking ahead while honoring history, Amarie anticipates future generations of eager undergraduate and graduate students as they explore academic and career opportunities, connecting scholars from across the globe and unifying learners through their shared admiration and commitment to French language and Francophone literatures. “The motto of Pi Delta Phi is very inspirational: «Avançons, amis fidèles de la culture française», which means, ‘Let us move forward, faithful friends of French culture,’” she said. “I like this motto because it emphasizes both growth (avançons) and commitment (fidèles) to French studies. We work together toward shared language, cultural traditions and values.”

title: Karol G’s “BbY WOW,” Sampling Iconic Coolie Dance Riddim, Tops Billboard Global Charts - Kaboom Magazine
content: Our latest digital magazine is available for download - CLICK HERE >> The Colombian Latin superstar’s collab with Judeline and Rusowsky dethrones Shakira and Burna Boy’s “Dai Dai” from atop the Billboard Global Excl. U.S. chart after generating 42.3 million global streams in a week and surpassing 103 million Spotify plays Colombian Latin superstar Karol G, alongside Spanish artistes Judeline and rusowsky, has climbed to No. 1 on both the Billboard Global 200 and Billboard Global Excl. U.S. charts with their collaboration, “BbY WOW.” The achievement gives Karol G her second leader on both global charts, following “TQG,” her collaboration with fellow Colombian superstar Shakira, which debuted at No. 1 in March 2023. For Judeline and rusowsky, “BbY WOW” marks their first No. 1 on either ranking. The track, which samples Jamaican producer Skatta Burrell’s iconic Coolie Dance riddim, has already surpassed 103 million streams on Spotify. According to Luminate, “BbY WOW” generated 42.3 million streams worldwide from August 28 to September 3, a 62% increase week over week, while selling 1,000 downloads globally, up 60%. The surge makes “BbY WOW” the biggest song in the world on Billboard’s global rankings, dethroning Shakira and Burna Boy’s “Dai Dai,” which previously spent 10 weeks atop Global Excl. U.S. and seven weeks at No. 1 on the Global 200. Released in 2003, Skatta Burrell’s Coolie Dance riddim has enjoyed a remarkable global reach over the past two decades, with its distinctive sound sampled and incorporated into music stretching from Latin America to India, the Arab world and the U.S. pop scene. The latest success also arrives amid renewed conversation around the influence of Jamaican production on global music. Iconic Jamaican production duo Steely & Clevie were recently dealt a major legal setback in their sweeping copyright case involving reggaeton’s signature Dem Bow riddim, after Bad Bunny and several other defendants secured a significant victory. title: GS Caltex to supply DHL Express with 2,000 tons of SAF - The Korea Herald
content:
Business GS Caltex to supply DHL Express with 2,000 tons of SAF GS Caltex will supply sustainable aviation fuel to DHL Express in Korea, expanding its presence in the fast-growing market for lower-carbon aviation fuels. The two companies signed a memorandum of understanding Tuesday at GS Tower in southern Seoul to cooperate on reducing aviation and logistics emissions through SAF. Kim Chang-soo, vice president of GS Caltex’s Mobility and Marketing Division, and DHL Express CEO John Pearson attended the signing ceremony. Under the agreement, GS Caltex will supply fuel for DHL Express aircraft operating in Korea for one year. The deal covers 2,000 metric tons of neat SAF, an unblended form of the alternative fuel that can be mixed with conventional jet fuel before use. The SAF was produced through co-processing, in which renewable feedstocks are processed alongside petroleum-based materials at an existing refinery. It has received ISCC EU certification for compliance with the European Union’s Renewable Energy Directive. GS Caltex will also participate in DHL Express’ GoGreen Plus program, which uses SAF to reduce air freight emissions. The program will cover all products shipped by GS Caltex through DHL Express. To meet growing demand, GS Caltex plans to expand its production capacity by completing a dedicated co-processing line by the end of this year, enabling commercial-scale SAF output. The refiner has expanded its domestic and overseas SAF operations since 2023. As part of a biofuel demonstration project led by the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy, it supplied fuel for Korea’s first SAF test flights with Korean Air. In 2024, GS Caltex exported SAF blended with Neste’s neat SAF to Japan’s Narita Airport through trading company Itochu. The deal made it the first Korean refiner to commercially sell SAF certified under ISCC CORSIA, an international standard for aviation fuels. The company is now working with Korean Air, Asiana Airlines, Jin Air, Eastar Jet and Aero K on certified SAF supplies. “This partnership with DHL Express marks another step in expanding our SAF customer base,” a GS Caltex official said. “We will continue to grow our biofuel business in line with market demand.” S.
